description: Telemetry for the AMD GPUs in this homelab, written against what these four cards actually report rather than against a datacenter reference platform. Every panel takes the union of the metrics the fleet supplies -- amdsmi where it answers, node-exporter's hwmon where it does not -- so a card is missing from a panel only when no source on that host can answer it. See the panel descriptions for which card is absent from what, and why.

panels.description:
Cards answering amdsmi on the selected hosts, counted from amd_gpu_health -- the one gauge every card in this fleet publishes, whatever silicon it is.

It counts cards, not hosts: a host with two cards contributes two. A card whose driver never bound is not here at all, which is the difference between this and the Exporter column on LAN Overview -- that one says the exporter is alive, this one says it found a GPU.
panels.title: GPUs Reporting

panels.description:
Package power summed across the selected GPUs, from whichever source each host has: amdsmi's average package power, its instantaneous package power, or node-exporter's hwmon reading for the amdgpu chip.

Three sources because no single one covers the fleet. amd-laptop is the only host with amd_gpu_package_power, snoc-strix only answers through hwmon for some fields, and snoc-gaming -- a Windows host whose GPU reaches WSL over /dev/dxg -- publishes no power at all and is simply absent from the sum.

Treat amd-laptop's single-digit reading with suspicion: under WSL amdsmi reports the dGPU slice it can see, not the whole package.
panels.title: Fleet GPU Power

panels.description:
The highest temperature any selected GPU is reporting, across edge, junction and memory sensors.

Deliberately a maximum over all three rather than one named sensor: they run 20-25 C apart on a loaded Navi 48, and the one that matters is whichever is closest to its limit. Drill into Thermals below to see which sensor and which card.

Thresholds are set for consumer Radeon silicon, where a junction temperature near 100 C is normal under load and memory can sit higher still. Red here means check the card, not that it is failing.
panels.title: Hottest Sensor

panels.description:
Correctable, uncorrectable and deferred ECC counts summed over every block the exporter reports, for the selected hosts.

All four cards here publish the whole amd_gpu_ecc_* family and all of it reads zero, which is the expected state: none of this silicon has ECC memory enabled, so the counters exist and never move. The panel earns its place as a tripwire -- any non-zero value is either a genuine memory fault or a card reporting something new, and both are worth knowing about.

Per-block detail is in the ECC table under Health.
panels.title: ECC Errors

panels.description:
Highest graphics engine utilisation across the selected cards.

Two different metrics feed this, because the fleet splits on which one amdsmi supplies: snoc-strix and snoc-thinkstation report amd_gpu_gfx_activity, amd-laptop reports only amd_gpu_gfx_busy_instantaneous (eight series, one per XCC, collapsed with max). snoc-gaming reports neither, and has no utilisation anywhere on this dashboard as a result -- its row is VRAM, ECC and PCIe only.

This is the gap the vendor dashboards fall into: they query gfx_busy_instantaneous for anything that is not a CDNA board SKU, which is exactly backwards for the two cards here that answer with gfx_activity.
panels.title: Busiest GPU

panels.description:
Framebuffer in use, summed across the selected cards.

The exporter reports VRAM in MiB and this panel is scaled as MiB, so 96 GiB of Strix Halo unified memory reads as 96 GiB rather than 98304 of something. Note that on the two APU hosts the figure is a slice of system RAM, not dedicated memory: snoc-strix reports a 96 GiB framebuffer carved out of 128 GiB of system memory.
panels.title: VRAM Used

panels.description:
One row per card, every column from a different corner of the fleet's telemetry. This is the panel the vendor dashboards could not be made to produce: they assume one silicon generation and one metrics source, and four of these cards are neither CDNA nor reporting the same subset as each other.

Blank cells are the point, not a fault. Read them as 'this card does not publish that', and the pattern is stable: snoc-thinkstation (Navi 48, bare metal) fills every column; snoc-strix (Strix Halo APU) has an edge temperature from hwmon but no junction or memory sensor and no amdsmi temperature at all; amd-laptop reports through WSL so it has power and activity but no hwmon and no temperatures; snoc-gaming reaches its GPU over /dev/dxg from WSL and publishes only memory, ECC and PCIe.

Temperatures prefer amdsmi and fall back to node-exporter's hwmon sensors, mapped the way the kernel orders them -- temp1 edge, temp2 junction, temp3 memory. That fallback is the only reason snoc-strix has a temperature here.

VRAM is the card's own framebuffer accounting in MiB. On the two APUs that is a reservation out of system RAM rather than dedicated memory, so a high percentage there means something different from a discrete card at the same number.

Identity, driver and ROCm versions are deliberately not repeated here -- they are on the GPU Inventory table on Home LAN Overview, which is the inventory view; this one is the telemetry view.
panels.title: GPU Fleet

panels.description:
Graphics engine utilisation over time, from whichever activity metric each card supplies -- amd_gpu_gfx_activity where it exists, amd_gpu_gfx_busy_instantaneous otherwise.

The two are not quite the same measurement. gfx_activity is an average over the driver's sampling window; gfx_busy_instantaneous is a point sample, so it is spikier and will read 0 between kernels on a card that is genuinely in use. Compare a host to itself over time rather than to its neighbour.

A host that never appears here is reporting neither, which today means snoc-gaming.
panels.title: GPU Busy

panels.description:
The non-graphics engines: memory controller (UMC), matrix cores (MMA), video decode (VCN) and JPEG.

Useful mostly as a division of labour. An LLM serving run shows up as matrix cores and memory controller moving together while the graphics engine does comparatively little; video and JPEG only move for media work, which on this fleet means essentially never.

Coverage is uneven and that is the silicon, not the dashboard: UMC and MMA come from snoc-thinkstation alone, VCN and JPEG from snoc-thinkstation and amd-laptop. An empty panel here is normal on an idle fleet.
panels.title: Engine Activity

panels.description:
Every process amdsmi can see with compute units allocated on a card, and how many it holds.

This is the panel to open when a GPU reads busy and nobody admits to using it. amdsmi reports the PID but no command name, so the answer is a number you then have to look up on the host -- the hostname column tells you where to run ps.

A process at 0 CUs is holding a context without currently executing: a loaded but idle Lemonade model looks exactly like this, which is why the row is shown rather than filtered out. Only snoc-strix and snoc-thinkstation report this family at all.

defaults.noValue: No process holds compute units on any selected GPU.

panels.title: Processes Holding GPU Compute Units

panels.description:
Framebuffer in use per card, in MiB as the exporter reports it.

The absolute numbers are not comparable across this fleet and are not meant to be: snoc-thinkstation and snoc-gaming are 16 GiB discrete cards, while snoc-strix and amd-laptop are APUs whose 'VRAM' is a 96 GiB and 32 GiB reservation out of system RAM. A rising line on an APU is pressure on the host's memory as much as on the GPU's.

All four cards report this family, which makes it the only live telemetry snoc-gaming contributes.
panels.title: VRAM Used

panels.description:
Framebuffer in use as a fraction of what the card reports as total.

The honest comparison across a mixed fleet, since the absolute MiB are not comparable -- but read an APU's percentage with care. Its denominator is a reservation the firmware chose, so 20% of a 96 GiB Strix Halo framebuffer is 19 GiB of system RAM that the host cannot use for anything else.
panels.title: VRAM Used %

panels.description:
Graphics translation table usage: system memory the GPU has mapped for its own use, as distinct from the framebuffer above.

On a discrete card this is the staging path -- buffers in host RAM the GPU reads across PCIe -- and a few tens of MiB is normal idle noise. On an APU the distinction is largely bookkeeping, since framebuffer and GTT are both system memory; amd-laptop sitting near a gigabyte while the discrete cards sit under 50 MiB is that difference, not a leak.
panels.title: GTT Used

panels.description:
Every temperature sensor the selected cards expose, labelled by which one it is.

Amdsmi first, node-exporter's hwmon as the fallback, with the kernel's sensor order -- temp1 edge, temp2 junction, temp3 memory. The fallback is what makes this panel work at all on snoc-strix, where amdsmi supplies no temperature whatsoever on gfx1151 and the vendor dashboards consequently draw three empty graphs.

Expect the three to separate under load: edge is the coolest, junction (the hotspot) runs well above it, and memory can be the hottest of all on a Navi 48. 100 C at the junction on consumer Radeon silicon is the card working, not the card failing -- it throttles long before anything is at risk.

amd-laptop and snoc-gaming publish no temperature on any path, because a WSL guest has no hwmon and amdsmi declines to answer over /dev/dxg.
panels.title: Temperatures

panels.description:
Power draw per card, from amdsmi where it answers and hwmon where it does not.

The three sources do not agree on what they are measuring and the panel does not pretend otherwise: average_package_power is a windowed average, package_power an instantaneous reading, and hwmon's amdgpu sensor reports whatever the driver chose to expose. Within one host the series is consistent and comparable over time, which is what this is for.

amd-laptop's reading is near 1 W and is not the laptop's real GPU draw -- under WSL amdsmi sees a slice of the package. Treat it as presence, not measurement.
panels.title: Package Power

panels.description:
Every clock domain reporting a non-zero frequency, by host.

The `> 0` filter is load-bearing. amdsmi pads its clock array out to a fixed length on some cards -- amd-laptop publishes eight 'system' clocks of which seven are a constant zero, and snoc-thinkstation reports a 'data' domain that idles at 25 MHz. Charting the padding makes the panel unreadable and teaches nothing.

Which domains exist is per-silicon: the Navi 48 reports system, memory, soc, fabric, dce, video and data; snoc-strix reports only fabric and dce, with no graphics clock at all. That absence is amdsmi's on gfx1151, not a missing query.
panels.title: Clocks

panels.description:
amdsmi's own verdict on each card, one tile per GPU.

It is a single bit and a blunt one: it goes unhealthy on conditions the driver considers disqualifying, not on a warm card or a full framebuffer. Everything else on this dashboard will tell you about a degrading card long before this does -- but if this ever reads UNHEALTHY, stop and read the kernel log.
panels.title: GPU Health

panels.description:
Any ECC block on any selected card with a non-zero count, correctable or not.

Empty is the correct and expected state, and the no-value text says so rather than leaving a blank panel that reads like a broken query. None of this silicon runs ECC memory; the exporter publishes the full 22-block family for every card regardless, all of it zero, so anything appearing here is new information by definition.

The filter is on the metric name, not a list of blocks, so a block this fleet has never reported still shows up the first time it counts something.

defaults.noValue: No ECC errors counted on any selected GPU.

panels.title: ECC Errors by Block

panels.description:
Current and maximum PCIe link speed as amdsmi reports them.

Only snoc-gaming and snoc-thinkstation answer, and the two disagree about units badly enough that the column is labelled 'as reported' rather than GT/s: one returns 32 where the other returns 2. Read each host against its own maximum and against itself over time -- a discrete card that has dropped a generation, or fallen to x1, shows up as a current speed well below the maximum beside it.

The bandwidth and error counters in the same family (amd_pcie_bandwidth, replay and NACK counts) are published by the exporter but carry no samples on any card here, so there is no panel for them. That is the exporter asking for fields this silicon does not supply, and it is why the vendor GPU dashboard has four permanently empty PCIe panels.

defaults.noValue: No selected GPU reports a PCIe link speed.

panels.title: PCIe Link
